Modern · The Seoul Table

Gochujang-Glazed Galbi Short Ribs

Slow-braised short ribs, a glossy gochujang glaze, and a little char at the edges.

Korean-American · Medium · Serves 4

Jump to recipe ↓

Behind the dish

Lane: modern — the paste's flagship argument. Thick English-cut short ribs, braised low in a gochujang-soy bath until the connective tissue surrenders, then glazed hard under the broiler: this is the record where the paste does all four of its jobs at once — it seasons the braise, sweetens the glaze, carries the ferment's depth through three hours of heat, and lacquers at the end. The grill-site's flanken cousin runs thin and fast; this build runs thick and slow, the Korean-American braise tradition with the paste in the driver's seat. Heat dial: 2, or 3 with the full gochugaru.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Sear the ribs first — the braise's floor. Salt the ribs (about 6 g), then brown hard on all faces in the oil, 8–10 minutes total. The fond at the pan's bottom is the braise's backbone; skipping it is the difference between a stew and a braise.
  • Cut the garlic and ginger heavy and smashed, not fine — they are aromatics for the pot and the strainer, not texture for the plate.
  • Marinating is not required in this build — the braise IS the marinade — but a 12–24 hour soak in a third of the braise ingredients (paste, soy, honey, pear grated) pushes the depth another notch. Choose by fridge schedule, not doctrine.

Let’s make it.

  1. 01
    The braise: seared ribs, aromatics, and everything liquid into the pot. The gochujang fried in the fond for 30 seconds before the liquids join (the bloom — the spine's first law), then soy, honey, mirin, pear, water, and the chilies over the ribs. Lid ajar, the barest simmer (a bubble every few seconds — 95 °C at the pot's edge, never a boil), 2.5–3 hours, turning the ribs once at the halfway mark. Checkpoint — the fork test at 2.5 hours: the meat yields to a fork's twist with no fight, the bone slides when pulled, and the braise smells deep-sweet-savory. Not there: 30 more minutes and check again. A boiled-tight braise means the heat ran — the low simmer is the recipe.
  2. 02
    Strain and reduce — the glaze is the braise, concentrated. Ribs out to a tray; the liquid through a fine strainer (the pear and aromatics have given everything — discard them), the fat spooned off the top, and the remaining liquid reduced at a hard simmer, 15–25 minutes, to a sauce that coats a spoon and holds a dragged trail. Taste: it should be intense — salty-sweet-fermented, a shade too strong alone — and then the extra honey and the lemon go in to round it. Checkpoint — the trail-holds test on the spoon, and the glaze's color gone from broth-brown to lacquer-red. This is the glaze the ribs are about to wear.
  3. 03
    The broiler lacquer. Ribs on a foil-lined tray, glaze brushed thick on all meat faces, and under a hot broiler (or a 230 °C oven's top rack) 3–4 minutes a side, watching through the door — the sugars go from lacquered to burnt in one careless minute. Two coats, two broiler passes, for the full build. Checkpoint — the surface: glossy, blistered at the edges, charred only at the corners — and a test pull at a bone-end strip should taste like the whole argument: the braise's depth, the glaze's sweet-heat edge, the char's smoke on top.
  4. 04
    Serve on rice with the remaining glaze at the table — there should be a small bowl of it, because the ribs' last act is dragging rice through the leftover lacquer. Checkpoint — the eating test: a bite of the rib's thick center with rice and the pickled crunch beside it — the meat should barely hold together, the glaze should announce the paste's ferment under its sweetness, and the pickle should reset the whole board. That triangle is the dish. Chef’s Note — the glaze's acid finish (that squeeze of lemon) is not optional garnish — it is the fourth quarter of the flavor. Three hours of braise builds sweetness and depth; the acid at the end wakes both up. Skip it and the glaze tastes heavy by the third rib; the same law runs the cho-gochujang dip and the chocolate tart (#14) at this site's other end.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The braise: seared ribs, bloomed paste, the barest simmer, fork-yield at 2.5–3 hours.
  • The glaze: strained, defatted, reduced to trail-holding, rounded with honey and acid.
  • The lacquer: two broiler coats, glossy and blistered, char only at the corners.
  • The table: rice, pickles, and the extra glaze bowl — the lacquer's drag is the dish's final course.

Finish & Plate

One or two rib blocks per person over rice, glaze brushed at the pass and the bowl of extra glaze at the table's center. Scallion threads and sesame over the ribs, the pickle plate beside, and spoons — this is a dish eaten with a spoon in the other hand.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Meat tight, not yieldingThe braise boiledBarest simmer; check at 3 hours, not before
Glaze burnt under the broilerUnwatched sugarsDoor open, eyes on, 3-minute passes
Glaze thin, soupyUnder-reducedHard simmer to the spoon's trail
Glaze one-note sweetMissing the acidThe lemon finish, always
Dial-3 heat never arrivedDried chilies were oldFresh gochugaru; taste the braise at the strain

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • The braise keeps 3 days refrigerated and improves; glaze-and-broil at the serving pass. The full glaze-braised-and-lacquered leftovers reheat under the broiler in 4 minutes — arguably the best office lunch in this entire corpus.
  • Variations: the grill-site's thin flanken cousin (kbbqguide#M04) for the fast fork; a spoon of the glaze thinned over the black cod (#11); dial up with fresh chili minced into the final coat.
